# The Main Loop

We have the canvas, the memory, the math, and the physics. Now we need to bring it all to life.

## Animation

Animation is an illusion. By changing the image on the screen 60 times every second (60 Hz), we trick the human eye into seeing motion.

In JavaScript, we use a special function called `requestAnimationFrame`. This tells the browser: "The next time you are ready to paint the screen, please call my function first."

[Why not `setInterval`? Because `requestAnimationFrame` pauses when you switch tabs, saving battery!]{.aside}

## System Architecture

Before we look at the code, let us look at the "Big Picture". The engine runs in three distinct phases:

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Input Scene] -->|Ray Query| B(Injection Phase)
    B -->|Energy| C{Fluid Solver}
    C -->|Advection| C
    C -->|Diffusion| C
    C -->|State| D[Renderer]
    D -->|Tone Map| E[Canvas]
```

## The Game Loop

Our `mainSimulationLoop` function is the conductor of the orchestra. It runs continuously, coordinating all the parts we have discussed.

```javascript
function mainSimulationLoop() {
  // 1. Handle Input (Keyboard/Mouse)
  if (handleInput()) {
      // If the user moved, we might need to reset
  }

  // 2. Injection Phase (Ray Tracing)
  // We shoot rays for every pixel (or a subset)
  // ...

  // 3. Propagation Phase (Fluid Dynamics)
  evolveSimulation();

  // 4. Rendering Phase
  // Draw the result to the Canvas
  // ...

  // 5. Repeat!
  requestAnimationFrame(mainSimulationLoop);
}
```

## Conclusion

We have journeyed from the humble pixel up to a complex, hybrid fluid-light transport simulation.

By treating light as a fluid, we can create beautiful, organic lighting effects that respond to the environment in real-time. We have optimised this by understanding how computer memory works (SoA) and by using simplified physics (Cellular Automata) instead of trying to calculate every single photon perfectly.

This is the power of the **Hybrid Fluid-Light Transport Engine**.
